title: Eli's Perfect Picture Day
markdown:
Eli the hedgehog stood in the echoey boathouse of Willow Creek Academy, far from his usual quiet hall at the Museum of Miniature Marvels, and the occasion sat heavy on his quills. The historical society wanted its annual photograph. He had polished, aligned, and worried over every stray leaf and misplaced acorn. His wish was modest and enormous: that the morning would pass without a single awkward moment.

“Mind the varnish,” he murmured, polishing a brass lamp until it threw a small sunbeam. He lined the rowing oars into a pleasing, orderly row, then squinted at the light, picturing the perfect angle.

A soft rustle announced Nora the hare. Eli’s quills twitched. Nora had organised the whole village fete. Her effortless efficiency felt, to his hesitant nature, like a quiet critique he had not asked for. She smelled of meadow and starch, and her ears moved as if they had their own calendar.

“Eli. Lovely to see you.” She carried a neatly wrapped bundle. “Extra polishing rags. I noticed you fussing.”

He had already polished the lamp twice. Competent people made his anxieties look ornamental.

“That is… considerate,” he managed.

Nora did not pause. “The asters by the entrance looked droopy. A few extra blooms for cheer.” She set them in a vase. Deep purple drank the light.

More flowers. An unsolicited improvement. He wanted to orchestrate every enhancement himself.

“They do look rather… vibrant,” he conceded, voice strained, because they did.

Mr. Abernathy bustled in with students. “Ah, Eli, splendid work! And Nora, how thoughtful with the asters. Perfect.”

Relief and injustice arrived together. It was impossible to feel a proper rivalry with someone so decent.

Students gathered. Whispers filled the boathouse. Eli smoothed his waistcoat and imagined the photograph: serene, dignified, his.

Then, as Mr. Abernathy called everyone together, a gust swept the open doors. Old exam papers lifted from a dusty shelf and swirled like papery moths. A crinkled sheet of Eli’s own scribbles snagged on his nose. He yelped. Composure went.

Before his quills could bristle, Nora plucked the paper from his face. In a blur she gathered the airborne sheets, stacked them, and returned them to the shelf. Seconds. The whole rescue, seconds.

Mr. Abernathy chuckled. “My word, Nora, you are a marvel.” His eyes caught a stripe of sun thick with dancing chalk dust. “Now, everyone stand still. That light is perfect.”

Eli, dazed, met Nora’s small reassuring smile. He had tried to control every thread. She had not controlled the wind. She had only tidied what it dropped.

The camera clicked.

“We appear to have organised a triumph by delightful accident,” Nora murmured, eyes sparkling.

Eli did not reach for the lamp again. He left the asters where they were, stood in the chalk-dust sun, and let the photograph take him as he was: a hedgehog with a neighbour, and a nose, at last, unpapered.
